questions.question: What is a breakpoint in the IDE debugger and how do you use it?
questions.title: Setting Breakpoints in IntelliJ IDEA
questions.direct_answer: A breakpoint is a marker on a line of code that tells the debugger to pause execution there so you can inspect the program's state at that exact moment.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic IDE proficiency — a developer who cannot use a debugger is very slow at fixing bugs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing how to set a basic breakpoint but not how to use conditional breakpoints or watch expressions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention conditional breakpoints — you only pause when a specific condition is true, very useful in loops

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A breakpoint is a marker I place on a line of code in IntelliJ by clicking the gutter or pressing Ctrl+F8. When I run the application in debug mode, execution pauses at that line before it runs. At that point, I can see the current value of every variable in scope in the Variables panel. I can inspect objects, expand them to see their fields, and even modify values on the fly. Once I've checked the state, I have choices: Step Over (F8) executes the current line and pauses at the next one; Step Into (F7) goes inside whatever method is called on this line; Step Out (Shift+F8) finishes the current method and pauses in the caller. A particularly useful feature is conditional breakpoints — I right-click the breakpoint and add a condition like 'user.getId() == 42'. The debugger only pauses when that condition is true, which is essential when a bug only happens for specific data.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Click gutter or Ctrl+F8 to set a breakpoint in IntelliJ
Run in Debug mode to pause at the breakpoint
Variables panel shows all in-scope variables at pause point
Step Over: execute line and pause at next; Step Into: enter method; Step Out: return to caller
Conditional breakpoints: only pause when an expression is true — essential for loops

questions.question: What is the difference between Step Over, Step Into, and Step Out in a Java debugger?
questions.title: Step Over vs Step Into vs Step Out in the Java Debugger
questions.direct_answer: Step Over executes the current line as a whole and moves to the next; Step Into enters the method being called on the current line; Step Out finishes the current method and returns to the calling code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical debugger fluency — can you navigate execution efficiently?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Stepping into library methods you don't care about and getting lost in framework code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Force Step Into (Alt+Shift+F7) to enter even library methods when needed

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Step Over (F8) executes the current line completely and stops at the next line in the same method. If the current line calls another method, that method runs to completion. I use Step Over when I trust that a method works correctly and just want to see the overall flow. Step Into (F7) goes inside the method call on the current line. I use this when I think the bug is inside that method. Step Out (Shift+F8) finishes executing the rest of the current method and pauses back in the method that called it. I use Step Out when I've stepped into a method and realized it's not where the bug is. A common mistake is accidentally stepping into standard library methods like ArrayList.get() — that wastes time. Step Over is the default for a reason.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Step Over (F8): run current line as a whole, pause at next line
Step Into (F7): enter the method called on the current line
Step Out (Shift+F8): finish current method, return to caller
Use Step Over by default; Step Into only when you suspect the method has the bug
Use Step Out to escape a method you stepped into by mistake

questions.question: What are watch expressions in a Java debugger and when are they useful?
questions.title: Watch Expressions in the Java Debugger
questions.direct_answer: Watch expressions let you evaluate and monitor any Java expression continuously as you step through code, showing the result at each pause point without adding print statements.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you use advanced debugger features vs basic ones only
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding System.out.println for every value when the debugger's Evaluate Expression panel does this without code changes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Evaluate Expression window (Alt+F8 in IntelliJ) for one-off expressions during a debug session

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Watch expressions in IntelliJ's debugger let me pin an expression and see its value at every pause point. Instead of just seeing individual variables in the Variables panel, I can monitor something more complex — like 'list.size() > 0' or 'user.getOrder().getTotal()'. I add them in the Watches pane, and every time execution pauses, the debugger evaluates and shows the current result. For one-off evaluation, IntelliJ has the Evaluate Expression window, opened with Alt+F8. I can type any valid Java expression and immediately see its value given the current execution context. I can even call methods, invoke constructors, or test logic there without changing any source code. This is much more powerful than adding a println.

content: Watch expression: a Java expression evaluated at every pause point in the debugger
Useful for deep object navigation: user.getOrder().getTotal()
Watches pane shows all watched expressions with current values
Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8): one-off expression evaluation at current pause point

questions.question: What are conditional breakpoints in Java and when would you use them?
questions.title: Conditional Breakpoints in Java
questions.direct_answer: Conditional breakpoints only pause execution when a specified condition evaluates to true — essential when a bug only occurs for certain data values, like a specific loop iteration or a particular object state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you've used debugger features beyond basic breakpoints — signals hands-on experience
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Stepping through 1000 iterations of a loop manually instead of using a conditional breakpoint
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention exception breakpoints — IntelliJ can pause automatically whenever a specific exception type is thrown

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Conditional breakpoints are extremely useful when a bug only manifests for specific data. The classic scenario is a bug inside a loop that processes a list of 500 items, but only fails for item number 347. Without a conditional breakpoint, I'd have to step through 346 iterations manually. I right-click the breakpoint in IntelliJ and add a condition: something like 'i == 346' or 'item.getId().equals("bad-id")'. Now the debugger pauses only when that condition is true. I also use them when a bug only happens for a specific user. Another related feature is exception breakpoints — in IntelliJ's Run menu under Breakpoints, I can tell the debugger to pause any time a specific exception type is thrown, even if it's caught somewhere.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Condition: any valid Java boolean expression evaluated at the breakpoint line
Essential for bugs in loops: condition like 'i == 999' avoids stepping 999 times
Useful for user-specific bugs: condition on userId or request parameter
Right-click the breakpoint in IntelliJ to add a condition
Exception breakpoints: pause when any instance of a specific exception class is thrown

questions.question: What is remote debugging in Java and when would you use it?
questions.title: Remote Debugging in Java — Basics
questions.direct_answer: Remote debugging connects your IDE's debugger to a Java process running on another machine or in a container, allowing you to set breakpoints and inspect state in environments like staging servers or Docker containers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of debugging beyond local development — shows production-awareness
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking debugging only works locally; freshers unaware of remote debugging look unprepared for real teams
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the JVM JDWP agent flag and that you'd never leave a debug port open in production

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Remote debugging allows me to connect IntelliJ's debugger to a Java application running somewhere else — like a staging server, a Docker container, or a different machine on the local network. The JVM supports this through a built-in debugging protocol called JDWP. To enable it, I start the Java process with a special JVM flag: '-agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=5005'. This tells the JVM to listen on port 5005 for a debugger connection. Then in IntelliJ, I create a Remote JVM Debug run configuration pointing at that host and port, and click Debug to attach. Once connected, I can set breakpoints, inspect variables, and step through code exactly as if the application were running locally. One important note: I would never leave debug ports open in production. A debug port gives anyone who connects full access to the running JVM.

content: Remote debugging connects your IDE to a JVM running elsewhere
Enable with JVM flag: -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=5005
IntelliJ: create Remote JVM Debug configuration with host and port
Use case: bugs that only occur in staging/Docker, not reproducible locally
Security: NEVER leave debug ports open in production

questions.question: What is a conditional breakpoint and when would you use one?
questions.title: Conditional Breakpoints
questions.direct_answer: A conditional breakpoint pauses execution only when a specified condition is true, allowing you to debug specific iterations or scenarios without stopping at every hit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical IDE debugger knowledge beyond basic breakpoints
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing conditional breakpoints exist and manually stepping through hundreds of iterations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example like debugging a loop that fails only on the 500th item

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A conditional breakpoint is a breakpoint that only pauses program execution when a specific condition you define evaluates to true. It's a powerful feature available in IDEs like IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse.

To set one in IntelliJ, you right-click on an existing breakpoint (the red dot on the left margin) and enter a condition expression, like `i == 500` or `user.getId() == null`. The debugger will then skip past that breakpoint on every hit where the condition is false, and only pause when the condition is true.

The most common use case is debugging loops. Imagine you have a loop that processes 10,000 items, and you know the bug occurs around item number 5,000. Without a conditional breakpoint, you'd have to press 'resume' 5,000 times, which is impractical. With a conditional breakpoint set to `i == 4999`, the debugger runs freely until it hits that specific iteration and pauses exactly where you need it.

Another use case is debugging null pointer exceptions when you only care about specific objects. You might set a condition like `customer == null` to pause only when that specific situation occurs.

Conditional breakpoints do slow down execution slightly because the JVM evaluates the condition on every pass through that line, even when it doesn't pause. So in very tight performance-sensitive loops, you'd want to remove them after debugging.

As a fresher, knowing conditional breakpoints exist and knowing how to set them will genuinely speed up your debugging on real-world problems.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Conditional breakpoints pause only when a Boolean expression you define evaluates to true
Set them by right-clicking a breakpoint in IntelliJ and entering a condition
Most useful in loops when a bug occurs only at a specific iteration
Slightly slower than regular breakpoints since the condition is evaluated on every pass

questions.question: What does 'step into', 'step over', and 'step out' mean in a debugger?
questions.title: Step Into, Step Over, Step Out
questions.direct_answer: Step Over executes the current line and moves to the next without entering method calls; Step Into enters the method being called; Step Out finishes the current method and returns to the caller.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of IDE debugger controls
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing step into and step over, or not knowing step out exists
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe a scenario where each action is most appropriate

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
These three controls are the core navigation commands you use when stepping through code in a debugger. Understanding when to use each one is fundamental to efficient debugging.

Step Over (F8 in IntelliJ) executes the current line and moves the debugger to the next line in the same method. If the current line contains a method call, Step Over executes that entire method without entering it — you don't see what happens inside. Use Step Over when you trust a method is working correctly and just want to move through the current method line by line.

Step Into (F7 in IntelliJ) also executes the current line, but if the current line contains a method call, it follows execution into that method. Use Step Into when you suspect a bug is inside a method you're about to call and you want to inspect what happens inside it.

Step Out (Shift+F8 in IntelliJ) runs the rest of the current method to completion and returns you to the method that called it, pausing at the line after the call. Use Step Out when you've stepped into a method and realized the bug isn't there — you want to quickly get back to the calling method.

Here's a typical workflow: you're stepping through a method with Step Over, you reach a line that calls processOrder(), you suspect the bug might be inside processOrder(), so you Step Into it. You look around, realize the issue isn't there, so you Step Out back to your original method.

Mastering these three controls makes the debugger much more efficient and precise.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Step Over: execute current line, skip into method calls — stays at the current method level
Step Into: follow execution inside the method being called on the current line
Step Out: finish current method and return to the caller at the line after the call
Use Step Over by default, Step Into to investigate suspicious methods, Step Out to exit dead ends

questions.question: What is the Watches panel in an IDE debugger?
questions.title: The Watches Panel
questions.direct_answer: The Watches panel lets you enter custom expressions or variable names that the debugger continuously evaluates and displays as you step through code.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only using the Variables panel and not knowing watches allow custom expressions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that watches can evaluate expressions, not just variable names

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The Watches panel in an IDE debugger like IntelliJ IDEA is a section of the debugger interface where you can add specific expressions or variables that you want the debugger to continuously track and evaluate as you step through code.

While the Variables panel automatically shows all variables that are currently in scope, the Watches panel shows only what you specifically add to it. This is useful when you're debugging a complex class with many fields and you only care about tracking two or three specific values — you add them as watches and they're always visible without having to scroll through a long list.

What makes watches more powerful than the Variables panel is that watches can evaluate expressions, not just variable names. For example, you can add a watch like `order.getItems().size()` or `user.getName().toUpperCase()` or even `items.stream().filter(i -> i.getPrice() > 100).count()`. The debugger evaluates that expression at the current point in execution and shows you the result. This saves you from navigating through nested objects manually.

You can add watches in IntelliJ by clicking the '+' button in the Watches section of the Debug panel, or by right-clicking a variable in code and selecting 'Add to Watches'.

As a fresher, using watches strategically lets you keep your important variables in view as you step through code, making debugging sessions much more focused and efficient. It's a small detail but it signals familiarity with professional tooling.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Watches panel tracks specific variables and expressions you choose, updated as you step
More focused than the Variables panel — shows only what you care about
Can evaluate complex expressions like method calls and stream operations, not just variable names
